title: Design Ticketmaster
summary: End-to-end walkthrough: TTL seat holds via conditional updates, idempotent payment, a virtual waiting room for hot on-sales, cached event pages and CDC-fed search.
body:
## Practice first

Design an event ticketing service. Fans browse and search concerts and games, open an event, pick specific seats on a map, and pay. For the biggest on-sales, millions of people arrive at the same minute for tens of thousands of seats.

Spend about 10 minutes before reading on: requirements, entities, the booking endpoints, a baseline diagram, and how you would stop two fans from buying the same seat. Then compare with the walkthrough.

## Functional requirements

Core (users should be able to):

1. **View an event** with its venue, date and seat map showing which seats are available.
2. **Search for events** by keyword, performer, city and date.
3. **Book tickets:** select seats, hold them while paying, and receive confirmed tickets.

Out of scope: event creation tooling for promoters, resale marketplace, dynamic pricing, refunds, and ticket transfer. General-admission (unseated) inventory is a simpler counter and is mentioned only briefly.

## Non-functional requirements

- **Consistency for booking:** a seat must never be sold twice. This is strongly consistent and non-negotiable; we will sacrifice availability of the booking path (show an error, queue the user) before we risk a double sale.
- **Availability and latency for browsing and search:** event pages and search favour availability and low latency (p99 < 500 ms); seat availability on the map may be a few seconds stale, because the final booking check is authoritative.
- **Hot events:** handle spikes of ~10 million users arriving for one on-sale of ~50,000 seats, without melting the booking database and while treating fans fairly.
- **Read-heavy:** browse/search traffic outnumbers bookings by 100:1 or more.
- **Durability:** a confirmed booking (payment captured) must never be lost.

## Back-of-the-envelope

- **Normal load:** say 100M events viewed/day ≈ 1,160 page views/s average, a few thousand at peak, and ~1M tickets sold/day ≈ 12 bookings/s. A single relational primary handles normal booking load easily. Decision: **no sharding needed for booking; spend effort on hot events.**
- **Hot on-sale:** 10M users in the first 10 minutes clicking seats every few seconds can generate ~100,000+ seat-hold attempts per second against 50,000 rows. Almost all attempts must fail fast. Decision: **meter admission with a virtual waiting room** so the booking service sees a rate it can serve, e.g. ~2,000 active shoppers at a time.
- **Event page reads:** a hot event page can see ~1M requests/s at on-sale. The static part (description, venue, images) is identical for everyone. Decision: **cache static event data at the CDN and in Redis**, and serve seat availability as a separate, briefly cached endpoint.
- **Hold duration:** if checkout takes ~5 minutes and 50,000 seats sell out, the system holds at most ~50,000 hold rows at a time; trivial to store, so the hold can live in the database rather than only in a cache.

## Core entities

- **Event:** id, performer, venue, start time, on-sale time, status.
- **Venue:** id, seat map (sections, rows, seats).
- **Ticket (seat inventory):** event id, seat id, price, status (`available`, `held`, `sold`), hold owner, hold expiry, version.
- **Booking:** id, user, event, ticket ids, status (`pending`, `confirmed`, `failed`), payment reference.
- **User:** identity from the auth system.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    EVENT ||--|| VENUE : at
    EVENT ||--o{ TICKET : offers
    BOOKING ||--|{ TICKET : includes
    USER ||--o{ BOOKING : makes
    TICKET {
        string event_id PK
        string seat_id PK
        string status
        string hold_owner
        datetime hold_expires_at
    }
    BOOKING {
        string booking_id PK
        string user_id
        string status
        string payment_ref
    }
```

One row per seat per event is the unit of contention. Every booking decision is a conditional update on these rows.

## API

```http
GET /v1/events/{eventId}
200 OK { "eventId": "e_1", "name": "...", "venue": { ... }, "startsAt": "...", "onSaleAt": "..." }

GET /v1/events/{eventId}/availability
200 OK { "asOf": "2026-11-01T18:00:03Z", "available": ["A-1-1", "A-1-2", "..."] }

GET /v1/search?q=jazz&city=Chicago&from=2026-11-01&cursor=...
200 OK { "results": [ ... ], "nextCursor": "..." }
```

```http
POST /v1/bookings/holds
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Idempotency-Key: 3c9f...
{ "eventId": "e_1", "seatIds": ["A-1-1", "A-1-2"] }

201 Created { "bookingId": "b_77", "holdExpiresAt": "2026-11-01T18:10:03Z" }
409 Conflict { "unavailable": ["A-1-2"] }
```

```http
POST /v1/bookings/{bookingId}/confirm
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Idempotency-Key: 5d0a...
{ "paymentToken": "tok_from_payment_provider" }

200 OK { "bookingId": "b_77", "status": "confirmed" }
410 Gone { "reason": "hold expired" }
```

Booking calls require auth and an idempotency key so retries after a timeout do not create a second hold or charge twice. The payment token comes from the payment provider's client SDK; card data never touches our servers. During a hot on-sale, booking endpoints also require a waiting-room admission token.

## High-level design

**Requirement 1, view.** The Event service serves event and venue data from a cache backed by the primary database; static event pages are also cacheable at the CDN. Seat availability is a separate endpoint so the large, static part of the page caches well while the small, changing part refreshes every few seconds.

**Requirement 2, search.** A search index (Elasticsearch or OpenSearch) holds denormalised event documents. It is fed by change-data-capture from the events database, so the database remains the source of truth and the index can be rebuilt.

**Requirement 3, book.** The Booking service performs a two-phase flow: **hold** (atomic conditional update moving seats to `held` with a 10-minute expiry) then **confirm** (charge payment, then move held seats to `sold` only if the hold is still ours).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U["Fan browser"] --> CDN["CDN (static event pages)"]
    U --> GW["API gateway (auth, rate limit)"]
    GW --> WR["Waiting room"]
    WR --> BS["Booking service"]
    GW --> ES["Event service"]
    GW --> SS["Search service"]
    ES --> RC[("Redis cache")]
    ES --> DB[("Postgres: events, tickets, bookings")]
    BS --> DB
    BS --> PAY["Payment provider"]
    DB -->|"CDC"| K[["Change stream"]]
    K --> IDX[("Search index")]
    SS --> IDX
```

Walk a booking: the fan opens the event page (CDN and Redis), fetches availability, selects two seats and calls `holds`. The Booking service runs one transaction that conditionally updates both ticket rows from available to held. If both rows change, it returns `bookingId` and an expiry. The fan enters payment details; `confirm` calls the payment provider with an idempotency key, and on success flips the two rows from held-by-me to sold and the booking to confirmed. If the fan walks away, the hold expires and the seats return to the pool.

## Deep dives

### 1. Never double-booking a seat (strong consistency)

**Bad: read availability, then write.** Two fans both `SELECT` seat A-1-1, both see it available, both write `sold`. Classic read-check-write race.

**Good: pessimistic lock across checkout.** `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the seat rows and keep the transaction open while the fan types card details. Correct, but it holds database locks for minutes, exhausts connections and leaves locks hanging when browsers close.

**Great: short atomic transitions with a TTL hold.** Each state change is one short conditional update:

```sql
UPDATE tickets
SET status = 'held', hold_owner = :booking, hold_expires_at = now() + interval '10 minutes'
WHERE event_id = :e AND seat_id = ANY(:seats)
  AND (status = 'available' OR (status = 'held' AND hold_expires_at < now()));
-- commit only if rows updated = number of seats requested, else roll back
```

Confirm uses the same idea: `SET status = 'sold' WHERE hold_owner = :booking AND status = 'held' AND hold_expires_at > now()`. Expired holds need no cleanup job to be correct because the predicate treats them as available; a background sweeper only tidies them for the availability view. A distributed lock in Redis with a TTL is a common alternative for the hold, but then the cache and database must agree; keeping the hold in the database that owns the seat avoids a second source of truth.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Fan A
    participant B as Fan B
    participant S as Booking service
    participant D as Postgres
    A->>S: hold A-1-1
    B->>S: hold A-1-1
    S->>D: conditional UPDATE (for A)
    D-->>S: 1 row, held by A
    S->>D: conditional UPDATE (for B)
    D-->>S: 0 rows
    S-->>B: 409 seat unavailable
    S-->>A: hold until 18:10
```

The database serialises the two updates on the row; whichever commits first wins and the other sees zero rows affected. No application-level lock is needed.

### 2. Payment and the hold expiring mid-payment (correctness across systems)

Payment is a remote call that can be slow, fail or time out ambiguously. Sequence matters:

1. Before charging, verify the hold is still valid and extend it slightly if needed (for example to cover the payment timeout).
2. Authorise or charge with an idempotency key derived from `bookingId`, so a retry never double-charges.
3. Flip seats to `sold` with the conditional update. If it affects zero rows (hold expired and someone else took the seat), **void or refund** the payment and tell the fan.
4. If the payment call times out, mark the booking `pending` and let a reconciler query the provider by idempotency key; do not release the seats until the outcome is known.

An alternative is authorise first, then capture only after seats are marked sold, which makes the failure path a cheap void rather than a refund. Either way, the booking row is a small state machine (`pending` → `confirmed` or `failed`) persisted at each step.

### 3. Hot on-sales: the virtual waiting room (availability under spikes)

**Bad: let everyone hit the booking service.** 10M fans hammer 50,000 rows; databases saturate, latency explodes, and winners are determined by retry scripts.

**Good: aggressive rate limiting at the gateway.** Protects the backend but produces random 429s; fans refresh constantly, generating even more load, and it feels unfair.

**Great: a virtual waiting room.** Before the on-sale, arrivals are placed in a queue (a Redis sorted set keyed by arrival time or a randomised position for those who arrived before opening). An admission controller lets users in at a rate matched to booking capacity, issuing a signed, short-lived admission token. The booking API rejects requests without a valid token. Queued clients get position updates via long-poll or SSE, which is cheap because the waiting room serves static-ish data. When inventory sells out, the queue is told immediately rather than letting people wait for nothing.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant F as Fan
    participant W as Waiting room
    participant A as Admission controller
    participant B as Booking service
    F->>W: join queue for e_1
    W-->>F: position 182,004
    A->>W: admit next 500 (capacity check)
    W-->>F: admitted, signed token (15 min)
    F->>B: hold seats + token
    B->>B: verify token signature and expiry
    B-->>F: hold created
```

The admission rate is the control knob: it is set from the booking path's measured capacity, so the database sees a steady load no matter how many people are queued. Tokens are signed so the booking service can verify them without calling the waiting room.

### 4. Fast event pages and fresh-enough availability (read scale)

Split the page. Static event data (names, images, venue, descriptions) changes rarely: cache at the CDN with a TTL of minutes and in Redis, invalidated on edits. Seat availability changes constantly: serve it from a Redis bitmap or set per event updated on each hold/sale (write-through from the Booking service or from CDC), cached for 1–2 seconds. Staleness here is safe because the hold is authoritative; the worst case is a fan clicking a seat that was just taken and getting a 409 with a refreshed map. For a hot event, push availability changes to admitted shoppers over SSE so they stop clicking taken seats.

### 5. Search with CDC (read scale and freshness)

Searching across millions of events with free text, filters and geo-distance is a job for an inverted index, not `LIKE '%jazz%'` in Postgres. Feed the index via change-data-capture (for example Debezium reading the write-ahead log into Kafka, consumed by an indexer) rather than dual-writing from the application, which can leave the two stores inconsistent when one write fails. Indexing lag of seconds is acceptable. Cache popular queries ("concerts this weekend in Chicago") for a minute at the API or CDN layer.

## What interviewers look for

- **Mid-level:** a working browse/search/book flow, a clear statement that booking needs strong consistency, and a database-enforced way to prevent double sales.
- **Senior:** the hold-with-TTL design using conditional updates, payment idempotency and the hold-expired-during-payment edge case, splitting static and dynamic page data, and CDC into the search index.
- **Staff:** treats hot on-sales as a separate system: waiting-room fairness and admission control tied to measured capacity, bot defence, graceful degradation, reconciliation with the payment provider, and operational signals (hold-to-sale conversion, admission rate, 409 rate).

## Common mistakes

- Checking availability in a cache and writing the sale elsewhere.
- Holding database locks across user think time or the payment call.
- Relying on a cleanup job to expire holds, so a slow sweeper blocks sales.
- Charging the card without an idempotency key.
- Dual-writing to the database and search index from application code.
- Using only rate limiting for on-sales, which rewards refresh scripts.

## Self-review checklist

- [ ] Seat state transitions are single conditional updates in the system of record.
- [ ] Holds expire by predicate, not only by a background job.
- [ ] Payment is idempotent and the expired-hold path voids or refunds.
- [ ] Static and dynamic event data have different caching rules.
- [ ] Hot on-sales are admitted through a waiting room at a measured rate.
- [ ] Search is fed from a durable change stream.
- [ ] You stated where you chose consistency over availability and why.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL: Explicit locking](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html)
- [Stripe API: Idempotent requests](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)
- [Debezium documentation](https://debezium.io/documentation/)
keyTakeaways: Booking chooses consistency over availability: every seat transition is a conditional update in the database that owns the seat.
Model checkout as a TTL hold that expires by predicate, never as a database lock held across user think time or payment.
Payment needs an idempotency key and an explicit path for a hold that expired mid-payment: void or refund.
A virtual waiting room admits users at the booking path's measured capacity, turning a stampede into a steady, fair load.
Cache static event data aggressively, serve seat availability briefly cached, and feed search from CDC rather than dual writes.
